issue.title: Could you please make the tag regularly after every update?
issue.body:
I made a Docker image of this project and update it regularly, but I don't notify about new updates!  
I can't build regularly in my CI/CD and unfortunately we are still using version v1.8.0!
Every once in a while, I checked this project and saw that there was still no new version (from the last tag) and I thought that this project was abandoned by Telegram and will not continue anymore!  Until today I randomly saw 21 new updates since the last tag that I didn't see and I was shocked!
https://github.com/Alwatr/containers/tree/next/tdlib

Could you please make the tag regularly after every update?

comments.body: If you want the tags to identify "the versions that are recommended to be used", then you just need to use `master` branch with the latest TDLib version as you would do for any other Telegram app, which are automatically updated. If you want to build the image regularly, but don't want to build it for every push to the master branch, then you can do this periodically, for example, once in a few weeks. See https://github.com/tdlib/td/issues/1790#issuecomment-991846880 and https://github.com/tdlib/td/issues/1627#issuecomment-885993462 for more details, why even some commits would be tagged `master` branch should be used instead anyway.

@levlam The answer was very strange and unprofessional and had nothing to do with my request!
Is there a specific reason why you don't update tags?

If you add me to the project, I will be honored to register and update the tags for you at the right time and even get a GitHub release to notify all those who started the project and make it more beautiful.

It is explained in the links that there is no "right time" for tags. Tag is just an alias for commit with some special meaning. If you need nothing special from the tag, then you can also use HEAD commit from the master branch always.

@levlam
I am very sorry to see this.
I think you are not familiar with usual GitHub release process and git flow release and even versioning at all!
I really did not expect this behavior from a professional project like tdlib! 
I apologize for taking up your time.
Please, if possible, at least delete all existing tags so that others don't make a mistake like me.
To do this, just run these commands in the command prompt
```shell
git push origin --delete v1.8.0
git push origin --delete v1.7.0
...
```

No, the tags are made on purpose. But as you should not use Telegram 2.5 (and you can't even download old app versions from any official distribution source), you should not use any old TDLib version and use the latest public version instead. If you want to run some Github action, then you need to run it on every public TDLib commit.
I'm create tag and release in this repository: https://github.com/njfamirm/td
you can use it, Also I'm interested to do this in current repo

> You should not use any old TDLib version and use the latest public version instead..

These words are completely true and I am successful with you, but believe me, regular release has its uses and is very beautiful and practical.
At least it makes everyone aware of the changes.
I think it is useless to continue this conversation.
I apologize again for taking up your time.
@njfamirm it's nice, thank you very much.

> At least it makes everyone aware of the changes.

Any new commit makes everyone aware of the changes made to the project.

> regular release has its uses

You provided no use cases for tags.

> users of apps that leverage tdlib on Void Linux will never have the most up to date version of the library. 

Each app version requires specific TDLib version and is incompatible with all other TDLib versions. See https://github.com/tdlib/td/issues/1718#issuecomment-953848719 for more details.

> [telega.el](https://github.com/zevlg/telega.el) specifically because it expects a version of tdlib greater than 1.8.20

Specific version of telega.el requires specific version of TDLib to be able to use its API. It is theoretically possible to support multiple TDLib versions by an app such as telega.el, but this would require enormous additional amount of work by the author of telega.el. Therefore, currently the distribution must provide dozens TDLib packages simultaneously, one for each TDLib version, from which only a few will be used by other packages. Is it an option for Void Linux package manager? Instead, apps usually bundle TDLib as it is done in https://zevlg.github.io/telega.el/#running-telega-server-in-docker.

Providing shared libraries as packages improves many things, for example, allows sharing of the same library between different apps, improving memory usage and performance, allows fast adoption of security patches by distro maintainers for libraries with stable API. Unfortunately, none of this can be applied to TDLib. If you want an opinion on the matter from a person you know, I can point you to https://lore.kernel.org/lkml/CAHk-=whs8QZf3YnifdLv57+FhBi5_WeNTG1B-suOES=RcUSmQg@mail.gmail.com/.

I see, thanks for taking the time to explain this.  I'm not sure if packaging multiple versions within a minor version range would be acceptable to Void (I'm not a maintainer, just a user) but my guess is that they'd prefer not to do it.  

I'll use an alternate approach to getting tdlib working for telega.el.  Thanks for linking the Docker image support, I was not aware of that!

What I want to mention is that an end user is unlikely to use multiple telegram clients in one computer at one same time.
So when using clients like telega.el, user may prefer to install the tdlib manually.
There's two reasons why using docker version is a bad solution:
1. It takes more computer resources just for one chat client.
2. For Apple Silicon chips, it need more steps https://github.com/zevlg/telega.el/issues/404 and may need Rosetta to work, which is not efficient.

If we have git tag, we may then build and install using https://docs.brew.sh/Versions to install the version we need like
```sh
brew install tdlib@1.8.25
```
Or make our own tap to build the latest version to keep align with the client's supported version.

Why to waste so much your and contributors time for a one second job?

The tags are easier to read and compare. Additionally with semantic versioning they allows to understand criticality of change. We always know that it should be safe to upgrade to the latest patch version.

For example, in the TG plugin for a Pidgin now [used a commit hash instead of a tag](https://github.com/BenWiederhake/tdlib-purple/pull/8/files/322e9dfa275bff3df3c958dd67ea01a98e359995..4c979bddfb2f8dcb8bcb225fd0ff4f8364394da5#diff-cdd48abbd3eb8d1c54077449fc74a8de1f29805d2be5d8e5232b7aab76ea7a6fL17) and this makes it harder to understand.

The GitHub provides a nice feature to see list of commits from the last release or compare between tags. I wanted to see it but I couldn't.

Telegram provides a lot of nice tools and I am grateful for both the platform and the APIs/tools. I understand that this is a lot to maintain and appreciate the effort. I can understand how yet another request which seems not so important can be annoying.

If there is a strong reason not to add tags to the GitHub repo, maybe another compromise would be to have a way to add version numbers to the automated build instructions (which are really nice, by the way). If that was OK, I'm confident that I or one of the other people on this thread would be happy to add a PR to support that.

Since [telega.el requires a specific version](https://github.com/zevlg/telega.el/issues/490#issuecomment-2295520364) of tdlib, I did the following as a manual work around:  I searched for `1.8.28` and found commit af69dd4397b6dc1bf23ba0fd0bf429fcba6454f6 as a hit. I then did a `git checkout af69dd4397b6dc1bf23ba0fd0bf429fcba6454f6` after cloning the repo and then followed the remainder of the automated build instructions.

I would still prefer to have tags for each release version, but if that is not feasible I think the above would be helpful for other users that need to build with a different version. Thanks.

Alex, we highly appreciate your work, but would you kindly implement some kind of release cycle? 
Or could you at least clarify what we need to use to build our bindings to your library?

We actually need it. If you let me take a bit of your time to read this I'll try to explain.

So, have a look please...
You updated tdlib to version 1.8.49 in this commit: [1](https://github.com/tdlib/td/commit/4a967f7a633d3c98184806650607b1746020a6a8)
We tried to build using this, but the builds were broken. So a couple of commits later your added this: [2](https://github.com/tdlib/td/commit/5140cf36bc2ea7e1d7eedf5471c2593bc92367b1)
And right now the HEAD of master is 7 commits ahead of the first commit where you updated the version: [3](https://github.com/tdlib/td/commit/51743dfd01dff6179e2d8f7095729caa4e2222e9)

What should other developers use to build their apps with? 1, 2 or 3? Now we know that definitely not 1. But we didn't know it when we started.

How should they know you released a new version as you just change a line in [CMakeLists.txt](https://github.com/tdlib/td/blob/master/CMakeLists.txt)? No way.

If you make some tags or maybe release branches, we could automate checking when you release anything, and configure our pipelines to build with it as soon as you release. It'd be very useful for example for such things like C# bindings for Telegram: [4](https://github.com/egramtel/tdsharp), [5](https://github.com/ForNeVeR/tdlib.native)

@freehck 

> but would you kindly implement some kind of release cycle?

The release cycle is known as "Rolling release": https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling_release.

> What should other developers use to build their apps with?

The developers should use the latest commit available on Github. This is the commit that is used in Telegram apps that use TDLib.

> 1, 2 or 3? Now we know that definitely not 1.

With this logic none of the commits should be ever used, because there are some newer commits. If you want to ship the most stable version without minor issues, then you can wait for the next commit with the message starting with "Update layer to " and use the previious commit. But doing this you will ship an already outdated version, which was used in production for about a month.

> How should they know you released a new version as you just change a line in [CMakeLists.txt](https://github.com/tdlib/td/blob/master/CMakeLists.txt)?

Every update in the master branch is more or less important. The change in the version signalize only about API changes, which are better to be monitored by examining changes at https://github.com/tdlib/td/blob/master/td/generate/scheme/td_api.tl.

> If you make some tags or maybe release branches, we could automate checking when you release anything, and configure our pipelines to build with it as soon as you release.

It doesn't harm to update on any new public commit.

Without releases and proper tags it is impossible to have stable and repeatable builds for dependent products. Checking out the master branch on every build is a nightmare - each build maybe broken. Of course, I can checkout with a specific git hash, but why not use a standard release procedure?

I was too tired of waiting for this to happen and decided to step up myself.

Here it is: https://github.com/ForNeVeR/tdlib-versioned

A repository that is essentially a copy of this one (check the `tdlib` branch), but with version tags.

Every day, it re-synchronizes with this repository, detects any commits that resulted in updating the `VERSION` in `CMakeLists.txt` (not by commit messages, but by actual commit contents!), and pushes the corresponding version tags.

To emphasize my good intentions, I added links to the explanation from the TDLib maintainers on why they don't want us to use the historical tags (so that people read that and, when appropriate, will go here and grab the latest version from `master` instead of relying on the tags).

Also, there are instructions on how to verify that the tagged code is genuinely an _exact copy_ (exactly the same commit hash) as this repository contains.

Hopefully it helps someone. Feel free to use that repository, contribute to the infrastructure, ask me any questions etc. etc.
@alimd, @ForNeVeR, I've also configured the [TDLib fork](https://github.com/g000sha256/TDLib) to automatically synchronize with the original repository, create version tags, and publish releases.
